description_ru: Эссе о том, как память не хранит прошлое, а переписывает его при каждом воспоминании, и почему это не повод для отчаяния.
text:
Somewhere behind the forehead of each of us there hangs a gallery, and in it, we believe, are displayed the authentic masterpieces of our lives: the first day at school, the wedding, the quarrel on the stairs, the summer of the broken bicycle. We stroll among these canvases with the serene confidence of a connoisseur, never pausing to ask whether the labels on the frames are accurate. It is therefore a little unnerving to learn from the laboratory that the curator of this gallery is a forger, a gifted and tireless one, who retouches every painting each time we visit it.

The evidence is by now considerable, and rather humbling. In the 1970s the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus showed volunteers films of car accidents and later asked them how fast the vehicles were going when they "smashed" into each other, or when they merely "hit". Those given the more violent verb recalled higher speeds, and a week afterwards many of them remembered seeing broken glass, although there had been none. A single word, injected into a question, had been quietly incorporated into the recollection. The memory had not been retrieved; it had been reconstructed, like a sandcastle rebuilt by every tide.

Neuroscientists have since given us a mechanism that is almost insultingly elegant. When we recall an event, the memory becomes temporarily fragile, and must be stored afresh, a process known as reconsolidation. In other words, remembering is not the same as consulting an archive. It is more like taking a manuscript from a shelf, copying it out from memory and then returning the copy to the shelf, while the original is quietly pulped. Each retelling is therefore an opportunity for revision, and the memories that we visit most often are, paradoxically, those most likely to have been altered.

Anyone who has attended a family reunion will recognise the phenomenon. Two siblings will argue vehemently about who pushed whom into the pond, each possessed of a clear and vivid picture, and each picture is incompatible with the other. Neither is lying. The brother has, over forty years, refined a narrative in which he is the wronged party; the sister has refined its mirror image, and both have been embellished with details borrowed from photographs, anecdotes and occasional wishful thinking. The pond, I suspect, has itself been enlarged by repetition, and has swollen from a puddle into a small lake.

The consequences in more serious arenas are sobering. Courtrooms depend on eyewitnesses, who testify with the conviction of men who have seen it all with their own eyes, and juries tend to find confidence persuasive. Yet research into wrongful convictions has repeatedly shown that mistaken identification is a leading cause of injustice, and that a witness's certainty increases as the trial approaches, since each rehearsal polishes the story. A confident memory, alas, is not a correct one. It is merely a well-rehearsed one, and the two qualities are no more related than a handsome cover and a sound argument.

Our first response to such findings is understandably defensive. If memory is so slippery, we are tempted to conclude, then the past is a fiction and the self is a sham. I should like to resist that despairing inference. The faculty that distorts our recollections is the same one that permits us to imagine the future, to learn from experience and to make sense of a chaotic existence. Memory did not evolve to be a faithful recorder, any more than the eye evolved to be a camera. It evolved to serve the living, and a living creature has little use for a literal transcript of everything that has ever happened to it.

Indeed, the capacity to edit is a mercy. The soldier who relives a nightmare, the widow who recalls a funeral, the child who remembers a humiliation in the playground: all of them benefit, over time, from the gentle softening of detail and the shifting of emphasis. Therapists can exploit this plasticity, helping patients to revisit a traumatic memory in a safe setting, so that when it is stored again, it comes back with a lighter charge. The forger, it turns out, is also a restorer, who works unceasingly to repair the damage that life inflicts.

None of this means that the past is a free-for-all. Our memories are not pure invention; the gist of them is generally trustworthy, and it is the particulars that wander. I remember that I was once lost in a department store as a child, and I am confident that I was frightened. Whether the store was a Woolworths, whether my mother wore a green coat, whether it was raining, I could not swear in a court, and I would be astonished if any of these details survived a determined cross-examination. The skeleton endures; the flesh is negotiable.

What does wisdom suggest, then? First, humility. When someone contradicts our version of events, we might entertain the possibility that we are wrong without being dishonest. Many a marriage has been saved by the admission that "perhaps I recall it differently." Second, a healthy respect for documents, diaries and photographs, which lack the charm of memory but also its talent for flattery. A letter written at the time of an event is a far better witness than the author of the letter, forty years later, will ever be.

Finally, a little tenderness for the forger. He is not our enemy. He is a fellow who has been at work in the gallery since we were born, retouching, restoring and occasionally adding a flattering sunset, and we owe to his labours whatever coherence our lives possess. A self is, after all, a story, and no story is told without being shaped. The only real mistake is to confuse the gallery with an archive, and to suppose that the painting on the wall is the thing that happened, rather than the thing that is still happening, every time we look. It is a collaboration, conducted without our consent and, on the whole, to our benefit.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Долгий нейтральный гласный: губы не округлены, язык в центре рта; не «ё» и не «о».
Рот открыт шире, чем для русского «э», звук короткий и напряжённый; не заменяйте на «а».
Дифтонг: начинайте с ɪ и плавно переходите к ə; не превращайте в долгое «и».
Тёмный звук l в конце слога: кончик языка касается дёсен, а задняя часть языка отодвинута назад; не мягкое русское «ль».

questions.question: Who showed that a single word could change how a car accident was remembered?
What is reconsolidation?
questions.answer: The process by which a recalled memory is stored again, and can be altered.

questions.question: Why does the author say that editing memory can be a mercy?
questions.answer: It softens painful memories and helps healing.
